whyCorrect: The text sets up a contrast between two ages of fossil: hominins (found in Asia) and the much older early multicellular organisms of the Ediacaran period. The word "because" asks you to explain why scientists have to leave Asia and go to Mistaken Point to find those older specimens. The only reason that works is that the Mistaken Point formation is older than the hominin-bearing formation, so it is old enough to preserve Ediacaran life. Notice the passage already tells you Mistaken Point is an Ediacaran formation, so the blank has to state what that means: an earlier time period.

whyWrong.A: The text never says North America lacks early multicellular organisms; it says the opposite, that Mistaken Point has them. It also would not explain why scientists must go there.
whyWrong.B: How widely distributed each type of fossil is says nothing about age, and the sentence needs an age-based reason for looking at an older formation.
whyWrong.D: Mistaken Point is presented as an Ediacaran site, not a hominin site, and preservation quality of hominins is irrelevant to finding organisms that predate hominins.

commonMistakes: Treating "look elsewhere" as a question about geography when the logical gap is about time.
tips: When a blank follows "because," state the reason in the same terms the sentence itself introduced — here, age of the formation.

whyCorrect: Track exactly what the study measured: personality traits and music-preference factors, in participants from fifty-three countries on six continents. It found similar correlations between the two in all those places. The conclusion that follows is simply that the personality-to-preference link holds across cultures — people with the same personality profile like the same kinds of music no matter where they live. The blank should restate the finding's scope, not extend it to something untested.

whyWrong.A: The study assessed preferences for Western genres only, so it gives no basis for predicting preferences for non-Western styles whose characteristics differ.
whyWrong.B: This compares the finding to what "researchers had previously assumed," but the text reports no prior assumption about how much the relationship varies.
whyWrong.C: Familiarity with Western music was never measured; participants reported personality traits and preferences, not exposure.

commonMistakes: Picking the most impressive-sounding claim rather than the one the described data actually supports.

whyCorrect: "Lawyer and cycling advocate" has no article in front of it, which makes it a title-like description that attaches directly to the name, exactly like "biologist Jane Goodall." A restrictive appositive of that kind takes no punctuation at all, so the whole phrase reads as one subject: lawyer and cycling advocate Ernesto Hernandez-Lopez has identified. Any comma inside it would break the subject away from its verb.

whyWrong.A: A single comma after "advocate" opens a nonessential element that is never closed, and it splits the description from the name it belongs to.
whyWrong.B: Two commas would make the name nonessential information, which requires a determiner like "the" before the description; without one, the name is essential.
whyWrong.C: The comma after the name falls between the complete subject and the verb "has identified," which is never allowed.

tips: No "the" before a job title usually means no commas around the name that follows it.

whyCorrect: The blank sits inside a dash-enclosed aside that already has its own opening and closing dashes. Within that aside, "the languages Javanese and Bikol" is a single noun phrase: the names identify which languages, so nothing separates the noun from the names. No punctuation belongs in the blank.

whyWrong.B: A colon needs a complete sentence in front of it, and "The Austronesian language family comprises some 1,200 languages—including the languages" is not one.
whyWrong.C: A dash here would close the aside far too early, leaving the rest of the parenthetical and the second dash stranded.
whyWrong.D: A comma would mark "Javanese and Bikol" as nonessential, but those names are the essential identification of which languages are meant.

commonMistakes: Adding punctuation because the sentence looks crowded; the dashes are already doing that job.

whyCorrect: Look at what surrounds the blank: "efforts that, through community involvement and scientific ___ aim to bring." The comma right after "that" opens a modifying phrase, and every such phrase needs a closing comma before the sentence resumes with its verb, "aim." So the blank supplies that closing comma: efforts that, through community involvement and scientific study, aim to bring adjutants back.

whyWrong.A: With no comma, the opening comma after "that" is left unpaired and the modifier runs straight into the verb.
whyWrong.C: A colon must follow a complete sentence and introduce something; here it would cut the relative clause off from its own verb.
whyWrong.D: A hyphen joins parts of words; it cannot close an interrupting phrase.

tips: When you see a comma just before an interrupting phrase, check that a matching comma closes it.

whyCorrect: The main clause is already complete: "such de jure judicial independence became more prevalent." Everything after "as exemplified in Croatia's constitution" is description hanging off the noun "constitution," and that description starts with the participle "enacted." The word joined by "and" must be another participle, so the blank needs "containing" — a constitution enacted in 1991 and containing four of these features.

whyWrong.A: "Contained" as a past participle would have to be passive, but a constitution does not get "contained"; read as a finite verb it has no subject.
whyWrong.C: "Had contained" is a finite verb with no subject available, since "constitution" is already the object of the preposition "in."
whyWrong.D: "Contains" is likewise a finite verb with nothing to serve as its subject, so the sentence loses its structure.

commonMistakes: Assuming "constitution" can act as the subject of the verb in the blank; it is governed by the preposition "in."

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with "While," which makes everything up to the blank a subordinate clause that cannot stand alone. The rest — "more than 80 percent of this endangered stork species is found in Assam, India" — is the main clause. A subordinate clause that comes first is joined to the main clause with a comma.

whyWrong.A: No punctuation runs the subordinate clause straight into the main clause with nothing marking the break.
whyWrong.B: A period would leave "While the greater adjutant can be found...in Cambodia" standing alone as a fragment.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and "While..." is not independent.

tips: A leading "While," "Although," or "Because" clause takes a comma, never a semicolon or period.

whyCorrect: Split the sentence at the blank: "One might assume cases like this...to be rare" is a complete sentence, and "they are counted among a litany of examples of Stigler's law" is another. "On the contrary" is a transitional adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot fuse two sentences. You need a semicolon before it and a comma after it: rare; on the contrary, they are counted...

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation before "on the contrary," the two independent clauses run together.
whyWrong.B: This puts the comma and semicolon in the wrong order, splicing the first clause to the transition and then cutting the transition off from the clause it introduces.
whyWrong.C: Two commas around "on the contrary" leave the two independent clauses joined by nothing but a comma — a comma splice.

tips: Transitions like "however," "therefore," and "on the contrary" need a semicolon in front when they sit between two complete sentences.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states a general finding: negative adjectives get replaced faster than other words. The second sentence applies that finding to a specific pair — the negative adjective "illegal" versus the noun "crisis" — and predicts what should follow from it. That is a conclusion drawn from the rule, so the transition must signal result.

whyWrong.B: "Moreover" adds a second, separate piece of evidence, but the second sentence introduces no new finding; it derives a prediction from the first.
whyWrong.C: "Meanwhile" marks something happening alongside or in contrast, and there are no two simultaneous situations here.
whyWrong.D: "However" signals contrast, but the example agrees with the research finding rather than complicating it.

tips: If the second sentence could begin with "so," the transition is a result word.

whyCorrect: The two sentences describe different dates and different eclipse types: 1904 gave a total eclipse where the Moon blocks the Sun completely, and 1935 gave an annular eclipse where a ring of light remains. The relationship is a contrast between two kinds of event, so the transition has to set the second against the first.

whyWrong.A: "As a result" claims the 1935 eclipse was caused by the 1904 one, which the text never suggests.
whyWrong.C: "Simultaneously" would mean the two events happened at the same time, but they are thirty-one years apart.
whyWrong.D: "Indeed" reinforces or intensifies the previous statement, and an annular eclipse is a different phenomenon, not stronger evidence for a total one.

whyCorrect: The previous sentence has just told you where the sculpture is: on the wall of a university building. The sentence with the blank then describes how it looks and functions in that place. "There" points back to that location and lets the description continue in the same spot.

whyWrong.B: "Later" would signal a shift in time, but nothing in either sentence marks a sequence of events.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would introduce a new example, yet this sentence is still discussing the same sculpture already named in the previous sentence.
whyWrong.D: "However" signals contrast, but the sentence confirms rather than complicates the point that Konrads's art blends into its surroundings.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is narrow: give the title of Hurston's first published short story. Only one choice actually pairs "first published short story" with the title "John Redding Goes to Sea." Everything the notes say about the year and the magazine is true but does not meet the goal, so a choice built out of those details fails no matter how accurate it is.

whyWrong.A: This gives the publication year and never states the title, which is the one thing the goal requires.
whyWrong.C: This supplies the year and the magazine but leaves the story unnamed.
whyWrong.D: This says the first work of fiction was a short story without naming it.

tips: Read the goal sentence first, then eliminate any choice that omits the specific item it names.

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize a difference between the two plants, so the sentence has to name both plants and state something true of one but not the other. Only one choice does that: it puts Pipturus albidus and Psidium cattleyanum side by side and separates them on native versus non-native status. The other options mention the plants without contrasting them, or discuss birds and seed dispersal instead.

whyWrong.A: This mentions only one of the two plants, so no comparison is made at all.
whyWrong.C: This describes the purpose of a study about birds and seed dispersal and never distinguishes the plants from each other.
whyWrong.D: This groups the two plants together as sharing the same trait, which is the opposite of emphasizing a difference.

commonMistakes: Choosing a sentence that mentions both plants without stating anything that separates them.

whyCorrect: The goal names one specific number to emphasize: Daniel Dias's gold medals. A sentence meets that goal only if it states the figure twenty-five and attaches it to Dias. One choice does exactly that, giving his total and then singling out the golds within it.

whyWrong.B: This gives debut years for both athletes and calls them multiple gold medalists without stating how many golds Dias won.
whyWrong.C: This is about Heinzmann and about what a gold medal signifies, not about Dias's count.
whyWrong.D: This gives Dias's thirty-eight total medals and his years of competition but never mentions gold.

tips: When the goal names a specific quantity, the correct sentence must contain that number.

whyCorrect: The sentence after the blank begins with "Instead" and says success usually comes through collaboration. That tells you the blank names the opposite of collaboration, matching the opening example of a prize going to a single person. "Solitary" means working alone, so recognition is not restricted to people who work by themselves.

whyWrong.B: "Coordinated" means working jointly, which is what "Instead" contrasts the blank with, so it reverses the logic.
whyWrong.C: "Considerate" describes being thoughtful toward others and has nothing to do with working alone or together.
whyWrong.D: "Coincidental" means happening by chance, which does not describe an individual scientist receiving a prize.

tips: Let "Instead" tell you the blank means the opposite of what follows.

whyCorrect: The narrator states the rule she was working under: she was supposed to memorize the whole piece. Right after "cheating" she explains what she did — looked up to see what notes followed instead of playing from memory. So "cheating" means she broke the requirement about how the piece was to be learned and performed, not that she wronged anyone.

whyWrong.B: No teacher appears in the passage and she is describing her private practicing, not an act aimed at fooling someone.
whyWrong.C: The contestants are never mentioned, and reading the music while practicing alone gains no advantage over anyone else.
whyWrong.D: She says she daydreamed and never listened, but nothing suggests she misjudged or misrepresented her own ability.

commonMistakes: Applying the everyday sense of "cheating" as deceiving a person, when the text defines it as skipping the memorization requirement.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank means what follows defines it. What follows is "a diverse range of musical talents in different areas, from orchestral pieces and operas to popular film scores" — a list of unlike kinds of music. So the blank must mean covering many different types. "Varied" is that word.

whyWrong.A: "Outdated" would say the music is no longer current, and the sentence calls the body of work impressive, not obsolete.
whyWrong.B: "Lonely" describes a feeling a person has, not a property of a catalog of compositions.
whyWrong.C: "Forgotten" would mean nobody remembers the work, which contradicts the praise and has nothing to do with range.

tips: A colon promises a restatement — read past it before choosing.

whyCorrect: Two clues fix the blank. Forrest admired Faulkner and wrote the passage "in tribute" to him, and the part after the colon says anyone who knows Faulkner would see the resemblance. A passage that deliberately reproduces another writer's style is an imitation of it.

whyWrong.A: "Forgetting" is the opposite of a tribute that visibly resembles the original.
whyWrong.B: "Rejection" would mean Forrest turned away from Faulkner's style, but he admired it and reproduced it.
whyWrong.D: "Opinion" is a judgment about something, and an opinion of a style would not produce a visible resemblance in the prose.

whyCorrect: The shortcoming is the narrow focus on North America and Western Europe, and the sentence says it came partly from limited data. Then researchers gained access to records from India and Hungary — data from exactly the regions that were missing. Getting the missing data makes the problem smaller, so the blank means to reduce or relieve it.

whyWrong.A: "Presuppose" means to assume in advance, but the shortcoming already existed and was being corrected, not assumed.
whyWrong.B: "Categorize" means to sort into groups, which does nothing to address a gap in coverage.
whyWrong.C: "Validate" would mean confirming the narrow focus was justified, the opposite of what new data from Asia and Eastern Europe does.

commonMistakes: Reading the new data access as confirming the old research rather than fixing its gap.

whyCorrect: Map the text in two moves. First it introduces the survey and reports the gap in park use, 71.9% in Bogota against 35.7% in Fortaleza. Then the last sentence raises one candidate explanation — better access to nonpark amenities near parks — and rules it out, because Bogota respondents actually reported less such access. That is a proposal-then-rejection structure.

whyWrong.A: There is one study covering both cities, not two studies, and nothing in the second half corroborates the first.
whyWrong.C: The text never blames the survey method; it rejects an explanation about amenities, not about how data were collected.
whyWrong.D: No open question about park planning is posed, and the text ends by eliminating an explanation rather than answering anything.

tips: For structure questions, label what each sentence does before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: The text spends its first half on El Museo del Barrio — when it was founded, what it is dedicated to, how large its collection is — and its second half on the Emma S. Barrientos Mexican American Cultural Center and what that institution focuses on. Nothing is argued or compared; the passage simply describes each one and its subject area.

whyWrong.A: Funding and how artworks were purchased are never mentioned.
whyWrong.B: No historical development is traced; the passage gives founding facts, not a cause that produced these institutions.
whyWrong.D: Only El Museo del Barrio's collection size is given, so no contrast of sizes is possible.

commonMistakes: Choosing a choice with a strong verb like "trace" or "contrast" when the passage only reports.

whyCorrect: The passage tells you what is typical of Erdrich: everyday life in Ojibwe communities. Then "Yet" introduces the exceptions, and The Crown of Columbus is given as one — adventure fiction set largely on a Caribbean island. The stated difference is therefore the setting, outside an Ojibwe community.

whyWrong.A: No film adaptation is mentioned anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: The amount of dialogue is never discussed.
whyWrong.D: Having Ojibwe main characters would make the novel like her usual work, not different from it, and the text does not say who the characters are.

tips: "According to the text" means the answer must be stated, not merely plausible.

whyCorrect: Follow where the paragraph lands. It defines horizontal gene transfer, notes it is common among prokaryotes, then says it can increase antibiotic resistance and that knowing how to prevent it might help control dangerous pathogens. The final clause is the point: studying this process could produce a practical benefit.

whyWrong.A: No common perception is described, so nothing is being corrected.
whyWrong.B: The text says the process is common but never compares that to what anyone initially thought.
whyWrong.C: There is no new research and no earlier findings being challenged.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that sounds like a research summary when the passage never mentions a study or a prior belief.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is specific: the PCFG whales' smaller maximum size is an adaptation to the resource opportunities in their particular foraging range. To support it, a finding must tie being smaller to getting food in that range. A finding that PCFG whales feed in shallow rocky kelp beds that larger ENP whales physically cannot reach does exactly that — small size is what makes those resources usable.

whyWrong.A: Proximity to ports and cities is about human activity, not about food resources or body size.
whyWrong.C: Different prey species show the ranges differ, but nothing connects that difference to why a smaller maximum size would be advantageous.
whyWrong.D: Trends in average size over recent decades describe change over time, not an adaptation to the foraging environment.

tips: A support question needs the choice that links the two specific things the hypothesis links — here, small size and access to food.

whyCorrect: The student's word is "must account for" — that is a claim that IGF-1 variation is the explanation for size differences among breeds. To undermine it you do not need to show IGF-1 is irrelevant; you only need to show it is not the whole story. Stating that IGF-1's gene is one of several genes known to affect dog size does that directly, because then size variance cannot be attributed to IGF-1 variation alone.

whyWrong.A: That most breeds do not share one variant just confirms the gene varies widely, which fits the student's conclusion rather than weakening it.
whyWrong.B: This limits how far the findings generalize to other species, but the student's claim is only about dogs.
whyWrong.C: This says the variations do produce substantial size variance, which supports the student instead of undermining them.

tips: Undermining an "X explains Y" claim usually means showing something else also explains Y.

whyCorrect: The claim is narrow: Vanya feels the professor does not appreciate him. Look for a quotation where Vanya says he worked for the professor and got no recognition for it. The line about managing the estate for twenty-five years, sending the returns "like the most honest of servants," and never receiving "one single word of thanks" states both halves of that claim.

whyWrong.B: This is Serebrakoff speaking about his own life and mortality; it says nothing about how he treats Vanya's work.
whyWrong.C: Vanya attacks the professor's scholarship as worthless, which shows contempt for the professor's achievements, not a sense that his own labor went unthanked.
whyWrong.D: This shows Vanya's disillusionment with the professor's career amounting to "a blank," again a judgment of the professor rather than a complaint about being unappreciated.

commonMistakes: Choosing any quotation where Vanya criticizes the professor, when the claim is specifically about Vanya's own work going unrecognized.

whyCorrect: The researchers' point is that climate change moves species into new ranges and makes previously unlivable areas habitable. If where a species belongs keeps shifting, then labeling one species native and another invasive rests on a fixed picture that no longer holds. The blank should state that general consequence: these classifications may not match the changing conditions.

whyWrong.A: International coordination is a policy recommendation the text never raises; the passage is about whether the categories still work.
whyWrong.B: Nothing singles out the Gaboon viper as the one case where the distinction fails; the concern applies to such classifications generally.
whyWrong.D: The text says the viper could outcompete native species in South Africa, not that vipers once lived there and were driven out.

whyCorrect: The first sentence states the purpose of the experiments: to better understand people living with PTSD. The findings are about why distressing memories persist for years. The contribution these results are expected to make therefore has to be to humans with PTSD, and the concrete form that takes is better treatment for them.

whyWrong.B: The mice were a model for studying human PTSD; understanding PTSD in the mice themselves is not the stated aim.
whyWrong.C: The connection between memory neurons in the prefrontal cortex is presented as already known and used to explain the result, so it cannot be the contribution the result makes.
whyWrong.D: More animal studies would be a next step in method, not the contribution the passage sets up with its opening purpose.

tips: When a text opens by naming its purpose, the conclusion usually returns to that purpose.

whyCorrect: "British artist" carries no article, so it works as a title attached directly to the name, like "British artist Chris Killip." That kind of description and name form one unit and take no punctuation between them.

whyWrong.A: A colon has to follow a complete sentence, and "A pet rabbit is held...by British artist" is not one at that point.
whyWrong.B: A dash marks a break or an aside, but the name is the necessary completion of "by British artist," not an interruption.
whyWrong.D: A comma would make the name nonessential, which requires a determiner such as "the" before the description.

tips: Description with no "the" plus a name equals no punctuation.

whyCorrect: Read both halves. "Some of these appear as lists" is a complete sentence, and "in 'Things That Arouse a Fond Memory of the Past,' Shonagon catalogs her appreciation for pressed silk, a moonlit night, and dried hollyhock" is another complete sentence that gives an example of those lists. A colon after a complete sentence is the right way to introduce that example.

whyWrong.B: With no punctuation, the second complete clause runs straight into the first with nothing separating them.
whyWrong.C: The colon lands after "in," cutting a preposition off from the title it governs.
whyWrong.D: A comma joining two complete sentences is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Assuming a colon must be followed by a list; it can introduce an explanation or example just as well.

whyCorrect: Everything up to "respectively" is one complete sentence about when the two paintings were finished, and "such allegorical artwork was particularly popular from the 15th through the late 18th centuries" is a second complete sentence. Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them need a semicolon, and "respectively" belongs with the dates it refers to, set off by a comma.

whyWrong.B: This ends the first clause with a comma and splices the two sentences together.
whyWrong.C: It drops the comma before "respectively" and still joins the two independent clauses with only a comma.
whyWrong.D: Putting the semicolon before "respectively" strands that word at the head of the second clause, where it has no pair of items to refer to.

whyCorrect: The sentence is building a three-item list of temperature readings, and the third item is already printed after the blank as the 8:30 p.m. reading joined by "and." So the blank has to supply the first two items with commas after each: the 3:00 p.m. reading, then the 5:00 p.m. reading, then a comma leading into "and." No comma belongs between a temperature and the time it was taken, because the time is not a separate list item.

whyWrong.A: Commas inside each item split the reading from its time, and periods would break the list into fragments.
whyWrong.C: Without a comma at the end, the second item runs into "and 16.2" as if two readings were one item.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon separates list items only when the items themselves contain commas, which these do not, and it cannot sit in front of "and" here.

tips: Punctuate each reading-plus-time as one unbroken item, then separate the items.

whyCorrect: Strip out the interrupting clause between the commas and the sentence reads "The chapter ___ known as Doo Alk'ai." The subject is "chapter," singular, and the surrounding sentences describe a present, ongoing fact, so the verb is "is." The plural noun "acres" sitting right before the blank belongs to the modifier, not to the subject.

whyWrong.A: "Are" is plural and agrees with nothing in the sentence; the subject is the singular "chapter."
whyWrong.B: "Have been" is plural as well, and the present perfect wrongly suggests a period of time rather than a current fact.
whyWrong.C: "Were" is both plural and past, and the chapter is still known by that name.

tips: Cross out anything between commas before checking subject-verb agreement.

whyCorrect: The blank starts a "from...to..." range: from one reading at 11:00 a.m. to another at 7:00 p.m. Nothing in that construction gets punctuation — "from" attaches straight to its object, and the object attaches straight to the time it was taken. So the blank takes "from" plus the temperature plus "at" with no commas at all.

whyWrong.A: The comma after "from" separates the preposition from its object.
whyWrong.B: It adds that same wrong comma and a second one that cuts "at" off from the time it introduces.
whyWrong.D: A colon cannot follow a preposition, and the trailing comma again splits "at" from its time.

commonMistakes: Adding a comma because the sentence is long; a preposition never takes one before its object.

whyCorrect: The previous sentence reports a success: NASA moved a moonlet's orbit. The sentence with the blank reports a limit on that success — nobody has shown the same works on a primary object like 2004 DC. That is a reversal of expectation, so the transition has to be concessive.

whyWrong.B: "For example" would make the second sentence an instance of the first, but a gap in the evidence is not an example of a successful test.
whyWrong.C: "Likewise" claims the two statements match, when one is a success and the other is an unproven case.
whyWrong.D: "Moreover" adds a further supporting point, and this sentence qualifies rather than reinforces.

tips: A sentence built on "have yet to" almost always needs a contrast word.

whyCorrect: The second sentence uses the past perfect, "had served," which places that presidency before the 1990 appointment just described. The transition needs to mark that step backward in time.

whyWrong.A: "In conclusion" signals the end of an argument, but this sentence adds an earlier fact rather than summing anything up.
whyWrong.C: "Thus" claims the NSBP presidency resulted from the National Science Foundation appointment, which reverses the order the verb tense establishes.
whyWrong.D: "For example" would make the presidency an instance of the 1990 directorship, but they are two separate posts.

tips: "Had" plus a past participle is a signal that the sentence is reaching further back in time.

whyCorrect: The paragraph makes a claim, admits something against it, then reasserts the claim. The blank sits at the admission: archways and mosaics obviously cannot grow in a forest. The next sentence opens with "Still," which is the signal that a concession has just been made, so the blank must be the word that grants that point.

whyWrong.B: "Thus" would present the sentence as a consequence of the architects championing nature, but it undercuts that claim instead.
whyWrong.C: "Furthermore" adds support, and this sentence raises a complication.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" claims a parallel between the two sentences, when the second pushes back against the first.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the "Still," in the following sentence, which is the clearest clue that the blank concedes a point.

whyCorrect: The goal names one thing to include: when the theory was published. Only one choice states the date, 1037 CE, and attaches it to the publication of the landmass theory. The other options are all accurate but leave out the one detail the goal demands.

whyWrong.B: This mentions the theory but gives no publication date.
whyWrong.C: This only identifies who al-Biruni was and never mentions the theory or its date.
whyWrong.D: This describes the theory and the scholar but says nothing about when it was published.

tips: If the goal asks "when," scan the choices for a date and eliminate every choice without one.

whyCorrect: To emphasize size, the sentence must state a measurement. Only one choice gives Tlaxcoapan's area, roughly 42 square kilometers, and identifies which place that area belongs to. Every other choice is about what a municipality does or where Tlaxcoapan sits administratively.

whyWrong.A: This is about street lighting as a public service and never mentions Tlaxcoapan or any measurement.
whyWrong.C: This places Tlaxcoapan among Hidalgo's municipalities, which is a count of regions, not a statement of Tlaxcoapan's size.
whyWrong.D: This describes the services Tlaxcoapan provides and omits its area entirely.

tips: "Emphasize the size" means the sentence has to carry the number.

whyCorrect: The goal is to indicate the title of the award-winning novel, so the sentence has to contain both the title and the award. Only one choice names Babel-17 and states that it won a Nebula Award. The others refer to a novel without naming it.

whyWrong.A: This calls a novel one of the best works of science fiction but never gives its title.
whyWrong.B: This describes Delaney as award-winning and names no novel at all.
whyWrong.D: This gives the publication year of an unnamed novel and never mentions the award.

whyCorrect: The sentence defines its own term: boredom "creates an anxious tension" when there is nowhere to fix your attention. The phrase "not somnolence but ___" then asks for the opposite of sleepiness, and the word has to name that anxious tension. "Perturbation" means agitation or unease, which is exactly what was just described.

whyWrong.A: "Fortitude" is courage under hardship, which has nothing to do with restless attention.
whyWrong.C: "Nonchalance" is unbothered calm, the opposite of the anxious tension the sentence describes.
whyWrong.D: "Indolence" is laziness, which sits on the same side as somnolence and so cannot be what the sentence contrasts with it.

tips: In a "not X but Y" frame, Y must oppose X — eliminate any word that is a near synonym of X.

whyCorrect: The adverb "eagerly" tells you the word describes a feeling, and the object is "the moment when he would be at home again" — something still in the future. Wanting a future moment to arrive is looking forward to it.

whyWrong.A: "Describing" would make the Mole narrate the moment, but he is hurrying toward it, not talking about it.
whyWrong.B: "Getting ahead of" is another real sense of "anticipate," but you cannot get ahead of a moment you are hurrying to reach, and it would not pair with "eagerly."
whyWrong.D: "Instructing" makes no sense with a moment as its object.

commonMistakes: Choosing a dictionary meaning of the word that the sentence's own context does not support.

whyCorrect: The paragraph is about where features of Puerto Rican Spanish came from — words from Taino, contributions from African languages. The example then links certain vowel pronunciations back to Yoruba. The blank names that act of following a feature back to its source, so "traced to" is the fit.

whyWrong.B: "Announced" describes making something public and cannot take "to how they are pronounced" as its object.
whyWrong.C: "Offered to" would mean presenting the pronunciation as a gift, which is nonsense here.
whyWrong.D: "Surrendered to" means yielding, not deriving from a source.

whyCorrect: The shortcoming is the narrow focus on a few North American and Western European countries, caused partly by missing data. The second sentence then says researchers gained access to records from Brazil and Russia — data from exactly the regions that had been left out. Getting that data reduces the problem, so the blank must mean to lessen it.

whyWrong.A: "Validate" would mean confirming the narrow focus was sound, the opposite of correcting it.
whyWrong.B: "Presuppose" means to assume beforehand, but the shortcoming was an existing flaw being addressed.
whyWrong.C: "Categorize" means to sort into groups, which would not reduce a gap in coverage.

whyCorrect: The flaw described is a focus limited to a few North American and Western European countries, driven by scarce data. New administrative records from Ivory Coast and Poland supply exactly what was missing, so the researchers' action makes the flaw less severe. "Ameliorate" means to make a bad situation better.

whyWrong.A: "Postulate" means to propose as a starting assumption, but the shortcoming is an established problem, not a proposal.
whyWrong.C: "Sanction" means to approve or authorize, which would endorse the flaw rather than reduce it.
whyWrong.D: "Rationalize" means to invent a justification for something, and gaining new data corrects the gap instead of excusing it.

commonMistakes: Reading the sentence as researchers defending the old research rather than fixing it.

whyCorrect: Follow the timeline the passage builds: bottles buried in 1879, bottles retrieved in periodic checks, results after 60 years, and another bottle dug up in 2021. The present tense in "researchers are conducting" and the 2021 retrieval both signal the experiment has not ended. The text's job is to lay out that long-running study.

whyWrong.B: Nothing here is about eliminating plants; the experiment tests how long buried seeds stay able to germinate.
whyWrong.C: Only one experiment appears, Beal's, so there is nothing to compare it with.
whyWrong.D: The passage reports results about seed viability but never discusses difficulties in preserving seeds.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences set up an apparent split: privately owned libraries with restricted access, then the first public libraries. The word "however" and Fernandes's point reverse that split — both kinds of owner treated their libraries as extensions of personal patronage. The passage exists to land that claim of underlying similarity, with the scale being the only real difference.

whyWrong.A: The text never claims private libraries disappeared, so it is not correcting that idea.
whyWrong.B: No judgment is made about emperors having too much influence; the point is about how both groups viewed their libraries.
whyWrong.C: Public access during the republican period is the setup, not the purpose, and the passage moves past it to Fernandes's argument.

tips: The sentence after "however" usually carries the main purpose.

whyCorrect: "Reductive" means a model boils something complicated down to too little. The energy ladder makes fuel choice depend mainly on one thing, household income. Heltberg's Guatemala study found use that was heterogeneous and flexible and shaped by several factors, including local prices. So the criticism is one cause versus many.

whyWrong.A: This says households ignore income entirely, but Heltberg's finding was that income is one factor among several, not that it drops out.
whyWrong.B: The displacement of one fuel by another is a detail of the model, and the text never claims fuel types are used in equal proportion.
whyWrong.C: The study is presented as showing fuel choice is complex generally, not as contrasting Guatemala's factors with Costa Rica's.

commonMistakes: Picking a choice that overstates the study's result into a flat denial of income's role.
